ROAD TRANSPORT (WORKING TIME) REGULATIONS 
The Road Transport (Working Time) Regulations (RTWT) requires employment businesses to 
maintain records of the Working Time of mobile workers who are involved in operations subject to 
EU drivers’ hour’s rules.  An employment business is obliged to ensure that the Working Time limits 
specified below are complied with for agency workers they engage: 
Summary of the RTWT Regulations: 
In summary, the RTWT Regulations provide the following: 
• 
Mobile drivers (such as HGV drivers and crew) are subject to a maximum average Working 
Time of 48 hours per week over a default 17 week reference period; this default reference period 
may be changed to a rolling reference period and extended to 26 weeks in certain circumstances. 
• 
There is a maximum weekly limit of 60 hours Working Time. 
• 
There is a maximum of 10 hours night work within each 24 hour period.  Night time is 
defined as midnight to 0400 hours (for goods vehicles) and 0100 and 0500 hours (for passenger 
vehicles).  This maximum may be extended in certain circumstances. 
• 
Rest periods – mobile workers MUST take the following breaks:  30 minutes after 6 hours 
Working Time and 45 minutes for over 9 hours Working Time.  It is important to note that EU Drivers 
Hours breaks and rest periods still apply. 
How we calculate your average Working Time: We will calculate your average Working Time over a

---

Hours breaks and rest periods still apply. 
How we calculate your average Working Time: We will calculate your average Working Time over a 
26 week calendar reference period.  The reference period we will use begins on midnight on the 
nearest Monday on or after 1 April, 1 August and 1 December each year and ending at midnight at 
the beginning of the nearest Monday falling on or after 26 weeks of these dates. Accordingly the 
reference periods are as follows: PERIOD 1 = 1ST JANUARY TO 30TH JUNE   [26 WEEKS] PERIOD 2 = 
1ST JULY TO 31ST DECEMBER  [26 WEEKS] 
First Call Contract Services operates a 26 week rolling reference period.

reference periods we use and to keep us updated as to any additional Working Time you undertake 
for other employers or employment businesses for these purposes during an assignment. It is also 
your responsibility to accurately record your Working Time during an Assignment. RTWT Regulations 
have been introduced to protect and safeguard the health and safety of mobile workers, other road 
users and the public.  A mobile worker also has a responsibility for complying with the Regulations.

If the mobile worker knowingly breaks the rules (e.g. neglects to inform his employer or employment

According to the working-time declaration, what is the maximum average weekly working time for mobile drivers?

answer:
According to the Road Transport (Working Time) Regulations, the maximum average weekly working time for mobile drivers is 48 hours over a 26-week reference period. This can be extended to a 52-week rolling reference period in certain circumstances.

- Summary:
  - Maximum average weekly Working Time: 48 hours
  - Reference Period: 26 weeks (extendable to 52 weeks in certain circumstances)

Process
[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by incorporating an information-retrieval mechanism that allows models to access and utilize additional data beyond their original training set. Ars Technica notes that "when new information becomes available, rather than having to retrain the model, all that's needed is to augment the model's external knowledge base with the updated information ("augmentation").[5] IBM states that "in the generative phase, the LLM draws from the augmented prompt and its internal representation of its training data to synthesize" an answer.[1]
RAG key stages
[edit]Typically, the data to be referenced is converted into LLM embeddings, numerical representations in the form of a large vector space. RAG can be used on unstructured (usually text), semi-structured, or structured data (for example knowledge graphs). These embeddings are then stored in a vector database to allow for document retrieval.
Given a user query, a document retriever is first called to select the most relevant documents that will be used to augment the query.[3][4] This comparison can be done using a variety of methods, which depend in part on the type of indexing used.[1]

---

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.[1][2] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
RAG also reduces the need to retrain LLMs with new data, saving on computational and financial costs.[1] Beyond efficiency gains, RAG also allows LLMs to include sources in their responses, so users can verify the cited sources. This provides greater transparency, as users can cross-check retrieved content to ensure accuracy and relevance.
The term retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) was introduced in a 2020 paper that described combining a parametric language model with a non-parametric external memory accessed through retrieval at inference time.[4]

Retriever-centric methods
[edit]These methods aim to enhance the quality of document retrieval in vector databases:
- Pre-training the retriever using the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), a technique that helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents.[13]
- Supervised retriever optimization aligns retrieval probabilities with the generator model's likelihood distribution. This involves retrieving the top-k vectors for a given prompt, scoring the generated response's perplexity, and minimizing KL divergence between the retriever's selections and the model's likelihoods to refine retrieval.[14]
- Reranking techniques can refine retriever performance by prioritizing the most relevant retrieved documents during training.[15]

The hypothesis is that by giving domain knowledge during training, Retro needs less focus on the domain and can devote its smaller weight resources only to language semantics. While RAG improves the accuracy of large language models (LLMs), it does not eliminate all challenges. One limitation is that while RAG reduces the need for frequent model retraining, it does not remove it entirely. Additionally, LLMs may struggle to recognize when they lack sufficient information to provide a reliable response. Without specific training, models may generate answers even when they should indicate uncertainty. According to IBM, this issue can arise when the model lacks the ability to assess its own knowledge limitations.[1]
RAG poisoning
[edit]RAG systems may retrieve factually correct but misleading sources, leading to errors in interpretation. In some cases, an LLM may extract statements from a source without considering its context, resulting in an incorrect conclusion. Additionally, when faced with conflicting information, RAG models may struggle to determine which source is accurate. The worst case outcome of this limitation is that the model may combine details from multiple sources producing responses that merge outdated and updated information in a misleading manner. According to the MIT Technology Review, these issues occur because RAG systems may misinterpret the data they retrieve.[3]

Process
[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language model
answer:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) adds access to external data sources to a language model beyond its original training data. This allows the model to incorporate new and relevant information in real-time, enhancing its capabilities in several ways:

- **Access to Updated Information**: RAG enables the model to draw from recent data, ensuring that the information it uses is current and relevant.
- **Domain-Specific Knowledge**: The model can include specialized knowledge from specific domains, which might not be covered in its training data.
- **Reduced Retraining Needs**: Instead of retraining the entire model with new data, RAG updates the model’s knowledge base incrementally, saving computational and financial resources.
- **Improved Accuracy**: By integrating external data, RAG can reduce the occurrence of hallucinations—where the model generates information that is not aligned with reality.
- **Transparency**: Users can verify the sources of information, increasing the transparency and trustworthiness of the model’s responses.

This combination of features makes RAG a powerful tool for enhancing the performance of large language models in various applications.

RAG and LLM limitations
[edit]LLMs can provide incorrect information. For example, when Google first demonstrated its LLM tool "Bard" (later re-branded to Google Gemini), the LLM provided incorrect information about the James Webb Space Telescope. This error contributed to a $100 billion decline in Google's stock value.[5] RAG is used to prevent these errors, but it does not solve all the problems. For example, LLMs can generate misinformation even when pulling from factually correct sources if they misinterpret the context. MIT Technology Review gives the example of an AI-generated response stating, "The United States has had one Muslim president, Barack Hussein Obama." The model retrieved this from the rhetorical chapter title "Barack Hussein Obama: America's First Muslim President?" in the book Faith in the New Millennium: The Future of Religion and American Politics.[6] The LLM did not "know" or "understand" the context of the title, generating a false statement.[3]
LLMs with RAG are programmed to prioritize new information. This technique has been called "prompt stuffing." Without prompt stuffing, the LLM's input is generated by a user; with prompt stuffing, additional relevant context is added to this input to guide the model's response. This approach provides the LLM with key information early in the prompt, encouraging it to prioritize the supplied data over pre-existing training knowledge.[7]

answer:
A RAG system can use new information without retraining the language model by incorporating an information-retrieval mechanism. Here’s how it works:

1. **External Knowledge Base**: The system maintains an external knowledge base that is regularly updated with new information.
2. **Document Retrieval**: When a new query comes in, the system retrieves relevant documents from this knowledge base.
3. **Prompt Engineering**: The retrieved information is fed into the language model via prompt engineering, enhancing the query with relevant context.
4. **Response Generation**: The language model generates a response based on both the original query and the newly retrieved information.

This approach allows the model to stay current without needing to undergo extensive retraining, thus saving computational and financial resources.

These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]

The model feeds this relevant retrieved information into the LLM via prompt engineering of the user's original query. Newer implementations (as of 2023[update]) can also incorporate specific augmentation modules with abilities such as expanding queries into multiple domains and using memory and self-improvement to learn from previous retrievals.[citation needed]
Finally, the LLM can generate output based on both the query and the retrieved documents.[3][4] Some models incorporate extra steps to improve output, such as the re-ranking of retrieved information, context selection, and fine-tuning.
Applications
[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation is used in applications where generated responses need to be grounded in external or frequently updated information.[citation needed]
In healthcare, RAG has been studied as a way to ground large language model outputs in external medical knowledge sources, although reviews have noted continuing challenges around evaluation, ethics, and clinical reliability.[8]

RAG and LLM limitations
[edit]LLMs can provide incorrect information. For example, when Google first demonstrated its LLM tool "Bard" (later re-branded to Google Gemini), the LLM provided incorrect information about the James Webb Space Telescope. This error contributed to a $100 billion decline in Google's stock value.[5] RAG is used to prevent these errors, but it does not solve all the problems. For example, LLMs can generate misinformation even when pulling from factually correct sources if they misinterpret the context. MIT Technology Review gives the example of an AI-generated response stating, "The United States has had one Muslim president, Barack Hussein Obama." The model retrieved this from the rhetorical chapter title "Barack Hussein Obama: America's First Muslim President?" in the book Faith in the New Millennium: The Future of Religion and American Politics.[6] The LLM did not "know" or "understand" the context of the title, generating a false statement.[3]
LLMs with RAG are programmed to prioritize new information. This technique has been called "prompt stuffing." Without prompt stuffing, the LLM's input is generated by a user; with prompt stuffing, additional relevant context is added to this input to guide the model's response. This approach provides the LLM with key information early in the prompt, encouraging it to prioritize the supplied data over pre-existing training knowledge.[7]

Chunking
[edit]Chunking involves various strategies for breaking up the data into vectors so the retriever can find details in it.
Hybrid search
[edit]Sometimes vector database searches (aka semantic search technique) can miss key facts needed to answer a user's question. One way to mitigate this is to do a traditional text search (aka full text search), combine those results to the text chunks linked to the retrieved vectors from the vector search, and feed the combined hybrid text (using effective scoring or reranking scoring) into the language model for generation.[18]
Challenges
[edit]RAG does not prevent hallucinations in LLMs. According to Ars Technica, "It is not a direct solution because the LLM can still hallucinate around the source material in its response."[5]

Retriever-centric methods
[edit]These methods aim to enhance the quality of document retrieval in vector databases:
- Pre-training the retriever using the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), a technique that helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents.[13]
- Supervised retriever optimization aligns retrieval probabilities with the generator model's likelihood distribution. This involves retrieving the top-k vectors for a given prompt, scoring the generated response's perplexity, and minimizing KL divergence between the retriever's selections and the model's likelihoods to refine retrieval.[14]
- Reranking techniques can refine retriever performance by prioritizing the most relevant retrieved documents during training.[15]
Language model
[edit]By redesigning the language model with the retriever in mind, a 25-time smaller network can get comparable perplexity as its much larger counterparts.[16] Because it is trained from scratch, this method (Retro) incurs the high cost of training runs that the original RAG scheme avoided. The hypothesis is that by giving domain knowledge during training, Retro needs less focus on the domain and can devote its smaller weight resources only to language semantics. The redesigned language model is shown here.
It has been reported that Retro is not reproducible, so modifications were made to make it so. The more reproducible version is called Retro++ and includes in-context RAG.[17]

Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.[1][2] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]

- Pre-training the retriever using the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), a technique that helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents.[13]

This involves retrieving the top-k vectors for a given prompt, scoring the generated response's perplexity, and minimizing KL divergence between the retriever's selections and the model's likelihoods to refine retrieval.[14]

[edit]LLMs can provide incorrect information. Without prompt stuffing, the LLM's input is generated by a user; with prompt stuffing, additional relevant context is added to this input to guide the model's response. This approach provides the LLM with key information early in the prompt, encouraging it to prioritize the supplied data over pre-existing training knowledge.[7]

How does the retriever select documents before the LLM generates an answer?

answer:
The retriever selects documents before the LLM generates an answer through several steps:

1. **User Query**: The user inputs a query.
2. **Document Retrieval**: A document retriever is called to select the most relevant documents that will be used to augment the query.
3. **Relevance Scoring**: The retriever scores the documents based on their relevance to the user's query. This can be done using various methods depending on the type of indexing used.
4. **Top-K Selection**: The top-k most relevant documents are selected for further processing.

This process ensures that the LLM has access to the most pertinent information before generating a response.

Does RAG completely prevent a language model from hallucinating?

answer:
No, RAG does not completely prevent a language model from hallucinating. Here are the key points:

- **Hallucination Risk**: RAG can still allow the language model to generate incorrect or misleading information, especially if the retrieved information is factually correct but misleadingly interpreted.
- **Context Misinterpretation**: The model might misinterpret the context of retrieved information, leading to incorrect conclusions.
- **Combining Outdated and Updated Information**: In some cases, RAG might combine outdated and updated information in a misleading manner, even if the sources themselves are factually correct.

These limitations highlight that while RAG improves accuracy, it does not eliminate the risk of hallucinations entirely.

Encoder
[edit]These methods focus on the encoding of text as either dense or sparse vectors. Sparse vectors, which encode the identity of a word, are typically dictionary-length and contain mostly zeros. Process
[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by incorporating an information-retrieval mechanism that allows models to access and utilize additional data beyond their original training set. Ars Technica notes that "when new information becomes available, rather than having to retrain the model, all that's needed is to augment the model's external knowledge base with the updated information ("augmentation").[5] IBM states that "in the generative phase, the LLM draws from the augmented prompt and its internal representation of its training data to synthesize" an answer.[1]
RAG key stages
[edit]Typically, the data to be referenced is converted into LLM embeddings, numerical representations in the form of a large vector space. RAG can be used on unstructured (usually text), semi-structured, or structured data (for example knowledge graphs). These embeddings are then stored in a vector database to allow for document retrieval.
Given a user query, a document retriever is first called to select the most relevant documents that will be used to augment the query.[3][4] This comparison can be done using a variety of methods, which depend in part on the type of indexing used.[1]

---

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
RAG and LLM limitations
[edit]LLMs can provide incorrect information. For example, when Google first demonstrated its LLM tool "Bard" (later re-branded to Google Gemini), the LLM provided incorrect information about the James Webb Space Telescope. This error contributed to a $100 billion decline in Google's stock value.[5] RAG is used to prevent these errors, but it does not solve all the problems. For example, LLMs can generate misinformation even when pulling from factually correct sources if they misinterpret the context. MIT Technology Review gives the example of an AI-generated response stating, "The United States has had one Muslim president, Barack Hussein Obama." The model retrieved this from the rhetorical chapter title "Barack Hussein Obama: America's First Muslim President?" in the book Faith in the New Millennium: The Future of Religion and American Politics.[6] The LLM did not "know" or "understand" the context of the title, generating a false statement.[3]
LLMs with RAG are programmed to prioritize new information. This technique has been called "prompt stuffing." Without prompt stuffing, the LLM's input is generated by a user; with prompt stuffing, additional relevant context is added to this input to guide the model's response. This approach provides the LLM with key information early in the prompt, encouraging it to prioritize the supplied data over pre-existing training knowledge.[7]
Process

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
RAG also reduces the need to retrain LLMs with new data, saving on computational and financial costs.[1] Beyond efficiency gains, RAG also allows LLMs to include sources in their responses, so users can verify the cited sources. This provides greater transparency, as users can cross-check retrieved content to ensure accuracy and relevance.
The term retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) was introduced in a 2020 paper that described combining a parametric language model with a non-parametric external memory accessed through retrieval at inference time.[4]
RAG and LLM limitations

---

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.[1][2] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]
How does hybrid search compensate when semantic search misses key facts?

answer:
Hybrid search compensates when semantic search misses key facts by combining traditional text search with vector database searches. Here’s how it works:

1. **Traditional Text Search**: Conducts a full-text search to find relevant documents.
2. **Vector Database Search**: Uses semantic search techniques to find similar documents based on vector representations.
3. **Combining Results**: Integrates the results from both searches.
4. **Effective Scoring/Reranking**: Feeds the combined results into a language model, using effective scoring or reranking to prioritize the most relevant documents.

This approach ensures that no critical information is overlooked, enhancing the overall accuracy and reliability of the search process.

How do sparse vectors differ from dense vectors in encoding text?

answer:
Sparse vectors and dense vectors differ in how they represent text:

- **Sparse Vectors**: These vectors encode the identity of a word, typically using a dictionary length and containing mostly zeros. They are more focused on indicating the presence or absence of specific words rather than capturing their semantic meaning.

- **Dense Vectors**: These vectors encode meaning and are more compact, containing fewer zeros. They are designed to capture the semantic and contextual information of words, making them more suitable for tasks requiring understanding of the text.

Both types of vectors can be used in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) processes to improve the efficiency and accuracy of text retrieval and generation.

Retriever-centric methods
[edit]These methods aim to enhance the quality of document retrieval in vector databases:
- Pre-training the retriever using the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), a technique that helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents.[13]
- Supervised retriever optimization aligns retrieval probabilities with the generator model's likelihood distribution. This involves retrieving the top-k vectors for a given prompt, scoring the generated response's perplexity, and minimizing KL divergence between the retriever's selections and the model's likelihoods to refine retrieval.[14]
- Reranking techniques can refine retriever performance by prioritizing the most relevant retrieved documents during training.[15]
Language model
[edit]By redesigning the language model with the retriever in mind, a 25-time smaller network can get comparable perplexity as its much larger counterparts.[16] Because it is trained from scratch, this method (Retro) incurs the high cost of training runs that the original RAG scheme avoided. The hypothesis is that by giving domain knowledge during training, Retro needs less focus on the domain and can devote its smaller weight resources only to language semantics. The redesigned language model is shown here.
It has been reported that Retro is not reproducible, so modifications were made to make it so. The more reproducible version is called Retro++ and includes in-context RAG.[17]

Improvements
[edit]Improvements to the basic process above can be applied at different stages in the RAG flow.
Encoder
[edit]These methods focus on the encoding of text as either dense or sparse vectors. Sparse vectors, which encode the identity of a word, are typically dictionary-length and contain mostly zeros. Dense vectors, which encode meaning, are more compact and contain fewer zeros. Various enhancements can improve the way similarities are calculated in the vector stores (databases).[9]
- Performance improves by optimizing how vector similarities are calculated. Dot products enhance similarity scoring, while approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) searches improve retrieval efficiency over K-nearest neighbors (KNN) searches.[10]
- Accuracy may be improved with Late Interactions, which allow the system to compare words more precisely after retrieval. This helps refine document ranking and improve search relevance.[11]
- Hybrid vector approaches may be used to combine dense vector representations with sparse one-hot vectors, taking advantage of the computational efficiency of sparse dot products over dense vector operations.[9]
- Other retrieval techniques focus on improving accuracy by refining how documents are selected. Some retrieval methods combine sparse representations, such as SPLADE, with query expansion strategies to improve search accuracy and recall.[12]

Process
[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by incorporating an information-retrieval mechanism that allows models to access and utilize additional data beyond their original training set. Ars Technica notes that "when new information becomes available, rather than having to retrain the model, all that's needed is to augment the model's external knowledge base with the updated information ("augmentation").[5] IBM states that "in the generative phase, the LLM draws from the augmented prompt and its internal representation of its training data to synthesize" an answer.[1]
RAG key stages
[edit]Typically, the data to be referenced is converted into LLM embeddings, numerical representations in the form of a large vector space. RAG can be used on unstructured (usually text), semi-structured, or structured data (for example knowledge graphs). These embeddings are then stored in a vector database to allow for document retrieval.
Given a user query, a document retriever is first called to select the most relevant documents that will be used to augment the query.[3][4] This comparison can be done using a variety of methods, which depend in part on the type of indexing used.[1]

It has been reported that Retro is not reproducible, so modifications were made to make it so. The more reproducible version is called Retro++ and includes in-context RAG.[17]
Chunking
[edit]Chunking involves various strategies for breaking up the data into vectors so the retriever can find details in it.
Hybrid search
[edit]Sometimes vector database searches (aka semantic search technique) can miss key facts needed to answer a user's question. One way to mitigate this is to do a traditional text search (aka full text search), combine those results to the text chunks linked to the retrieved vectors from the vector search, and feed the combined hybrid text (using effective scoring or reranking scoring) into the language model for generation.[18]
Challenges
[edit]RAG does not prevent hallucinations in LLMs. According to Ars Technica, "It is not a direct solution because the LLM can still hallucinate around the source material in its response."[5]

The model feeds this relevant retrieved information into the LLM via prompt engineering of the user's original query. Newer implementations (as of 2023[update]) can also incorporate specific augmentation modules with abilities such as expanding queries into multiple domains and using memory and self-improvement to learn from previous retrievals.[citation needed]
Finally, the LLM can generate output based on both the query and the retrieved documents.[3][4] Some models incorporate extra steps to improve output, such as the re-ranking of retrieved information, context selection, and fine-tuning.
Applications
[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation is used in applications where generated responses need to be grounded in external or frequently updated information.[citation needed]
In healthcare, RAG has been studied as a way to ground large language model outputs in external medical knowledge sources, although reviews have noted continuing challenges around evaluation, ethics, and clinical reliability.[8]

Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.[1][2] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]
What pre-training task teaches a retriever to predict masked text?

answer:
The pre-training task that teaches a retriever to predict masked text is the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT).

This task helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents, enhancing its ability to understand and retrieve relevant information.

[edit]RAG does not prevent hallucinations in LLMs. According to Ars Technica, "It is not a direct solution because the LLM can still hallucinate around the source material in its response."[5]
While RAG improves the accuracy of large language models (LLMs), it does not eliminate all challenges. One limitation is that while RAG reduces the need for frequent model retraining, it does not remove it entirely. Additionally, LLMs may struggle to recognize when they lack sufficient information to provide a reliable response. Without specific training, models may generate answers even when they should indicate uncertainty. According to IBM, this issue can arise when the model lacks the ability to assess its own knowledge limitations.[1]
RAG poisoning
[edit]RAG systems may retrieve factually correct but misleading sources, leading to errors in interpretation. In some cases, an LLM may extract statements from a source without considering its context, resulting in an incorrect conclusion. Additionally, when faced with conflicting information, RAG models may struggle to determine which source is accurate. The worst case outcome of this limitation is that the model may combine details from multiple sources producing responses that merge outdated and updated information in a misleading manner. According to the MIT Technology Review, these issues occur because RAG systems may misinterpret the data they retrieve.[3]

[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by incorporating an information-retrieval mechanism that allows models to access and utilize additional data beyond their original training set. Ars Technica notes that "when new information becomes available, rather than having to retrain the model, all that's needed is to augment the model's external knowledge base with the updated information ("augmentation").[5] IBM states that "in the generative phase, the LLM draws from the augmented prompt and its internal representation of its training data to synthesize" an answer.[1]
RAG key stages
[edit]Typically, the data to be referenced is converted into LLM embeddings, numerical representations in the form of a large vector space. RAG can be used on unstructured (usually text), semi-structured, or structured data (for example knowledge graphs). These embeddings are then stored in a vector database to allow for document retrieval.
Given a user query, a document retriever is first called to select the most relevant documents that will be used to augment the query.[3][4] This comparison can be done using a variety of methods, which depend in part on the type of indexing used.[1]

[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation is used in applications where generated responses need to be grounded in external or frequently updated information.[citation needed]

[edit]Improvements to the basic process above can be applied at different stages in the RAG flow.
Encoder
[edit]These methods focus on the encoding of text as either dense or sparse vectors. Sparse vectors, which encode the identity of a word, are typically dictionary-length and contain mostly zeros. Dense vectors, which encode meaning, are more compact and contain fewer zeros. Various enhancements can improve the way similarities are calculated in the vector stores (databases).[9]
- Performance improves by optimizing how vector similarities are calculated. Dot products enhance similarity scoring, while approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) searches improve retrieval efficiency over K-nearest neighbors (KNN) searches.[10]
- Accuracy may be improved with Late Interactions, which allow the system to compare words more precisely after retrieval. This helps refine document ranking and improve search relevance.[11]
- Hybrid vector approaches may be used to combine dense vector representations with sparse one-hot vectors, taking advantage of the computational efficiency of sparse dot products over dense vector operations.[9]
- Other retrieval techniques focus on improving accuracy by refining how documents are selected. Some retrieval methods combine sparse representations, such as SPLADE, with query expansion strategies to improve search accuracy and recall.[12]
Retriever-centric methods

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
Retriever-centric methods
[edit]These methods aim to enhance the quality of document retrieval in vector databases:
- Pre-training the retriever using the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), a technique that helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents.[13]
- Supervised retriever optimization aligns retrieval probabilities with the generator model's likelihood distribution. This involves retrieving the top-k vectors for a given prompt, scoring the generated response's perplexity, and minimizing KL divergence between the retriever's selections and the model's likelihoods to refine retrieval.[14]
- Reranking techniques can refine retriever performance by prioritizing the most relevant retrieved documents during training.[15]

Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.[1][2] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]

LLMs with RAG are programmed to prioritize new information. This technique has been called "prompt stuffing." Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.[1][2] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. Can a model still answer incorrectly when RAG retrieves factually correct material, and why?

expected_facts: Yes. The model can misinterpret the context even when retrieved sources are factually correct.
answer:
Yes, a model can still answer incorrectly even when RAG retrieves factually correct material. Here’s why:

- **Misinterpretation of Context**: Even if the retrieved material is factually correct, the model might misinterpret the context. For example, it might extract statements without considering the broader context, leading to incorrect conclusions.

- **Handling Conflicting Information**: When faced with conflicting information, RAG models might struggle to determine which source is accurate. This can result in combining outdated and updated information in a misleading manner.

- **Lack of Self-Awareness**: Models may not recognize when they lack sufficient information to provide a reliable response. They might generate answers even when they should indicate uncertainty.

- **Prompt Stuffing**: To mitigate some of these issues, models are sometimes programmed to prioritize new information through techniques like "prompt stuffing." However, this can introduce its own biases and inaccuracies.

These factors highlight the ongoing challenges in ensuring the accuracy and reliability of AI-generated responses, even with advanced retrieval mechanisms.

Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.[1][2] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]

answer:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by allowing them to access and utilize additional data beyond their original training set. This is achieved through an information-retrieval mechanism that converts data into LLM embeddings and stores them in a vector database.

### Key Stages of RAG
1. **Data Conversion**: Relevant documents are converted into LLM embeddings, which are numerical representations in a large vector space.
2. **Document Retrieval**: Given a user query, a document retriever selects the most relevant documents to augment the query.
3. **Prompt Engineering**: The retrieved information is fed into the LLM via prompt engineering of the user’s original query.
4. **Response Generation**: The LLM generates output based on both the query and the retrieved documents, sometimes incorporating extra steps like re-ranking and fine-tuning.

### Benefits of RAG
- **Efficiency**: Reduces the need to retrain LLMs with new data, saving computational and financial costs.
- **Transparency**: Allows LLMs to include sources in their responses, enabling users to verify cited sources.
- **Improved Accuracy**: Helps reduce AI hallucinations by grounding responses in external or frequently updated information.

### Limitations of RAG
- **Hallucinations**: RAG does not prevent LLMs from hallucinating around the source material in their responses.
- **Evaluation Challenges**: Ongoing issues with evaluating the effectiveness and reliability of RAG in real-world applications.
- **Ethical Concerns**: Potential ethical implications, especially when used for biased or misleading content.

This summary captures the core mechanics, advantages, and drawbacks of RAG as described in the provided context.

answer:
### Origin of RAG
RAG was introduced in a 2020 paper that combined a parametric language model with a non-parametric external memory accessed through retrieval at inference time. This technique aims to enhance large language models (LLMs) by allowing them to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.

### Retrieval and Augmentation Process
1. **Data Conversion**: The data to be referenced is converted into LLM embeddings, which are numerical representations in a large vector space.
2. **Vector Database Storage**: These embeddings are stored in a vector database to facilitate document retrieval.
3. **Query Processing**: Given a user query, a document retriever selects the most relevant documents to augment the query.
4. **LLM Integration**: The LLM then draws from the augmented prompt and its internal representation of training data to synthesize an answer.

### Data Sources
- **Structured Data**: Knowledge graphs.
- **Unstructured Data**: Text documents.
- **External Databases**: Web sources, uploaded documents, or other databases.

### Limitations
1. **Hallucinations**: RAG does not prevent LLMs from hallucinating around the source material in their responses.
2. **Evaluation Challenges**: There are ongoing issues with evaluating the effectiveness and reliability of RAG.
3. **Ethical Concerns**: Ethical considerations remain a challenge, especially in applications like healthcare.
4. **Contextual Understanding**: LLMs may struggle to recognize when they lack sufficient information to provide a reliable response.
5. **RAG Poisoning**: Factually correct but misleading sources can be retrieved, leading to errors in interpretation.
6. **Cost and Reproducibility**: Some models like Retro are not reproducible, requiring modifications to ensure consistency.

These aspects highlight the strengths and weaknesses of RAG in enhancing LLMs with external data.

answer:
RAG can significantly improve answer grounding by incorporating external data sources into the responses generated by large language models (LLMs). However, there are limitations to what RAG can achieve:

### What RAG Can Do:
- **Enhance Accuracy**: By retrieving and integrating relevant information from external sources, RAG can provide more accurate and up-to-date answers compared to relying solely on the LLM’s pre-existing training data.
- **Support Verification**: The inclusion of cited sources allows users to verify the information, enhancing transparency and trust in the responses.
- **Reduce Hallucinations**: RAG can help reduce instances where LLMs generate false or misleading information, as the retrieved sources can serve as a factual check.

### What RAG Cannot Do:
- **Eliminate Hallucinations Completely**: Despite reducing the likelihood of hallucinations, RAG does not guarantee that LLMs will never generate false information.
- **Ensure Perfect Context Understanding**: Even with retrieved sources, LLMs may still misinterpret the context, leading to incorrect conclusions.
- **Prevent RAG Poisoning**: RAG systems can retrieve factually correct but misleading sources, which can lead to errors in interpretation.

### How Retrieved Sources Support Verification:
- **Cited Sources**: By including cited sources in the responses, RAG allows users to cross-check the information against the original documents.
- **Transparency**: This practice increases transparency, enabling users to assess the credibility and relevance of the retrieved information.
- **Cross-Checking**: Users can verify the accuracy and relevance of the retrieved content, ensuring that the LLM’s responses are grounded in reliable sources.

### Summary:
RAG enhances answer grounding by integrating external data sources, which improves accuracy and supports verification. However, it cannot completely eliminate hallucinations or ensure perfect context understanding. The inclusion of cited sources in responses enhances transparency and allows for cross-checking, but RAG remains subject to limitations such as RAG poisoning and potential misinterpretation of context.

Improvements
[edit]Improvements to the basic process above can be applied at different stages in the RAG flow.
Encoder
[edit]These methods focus on the encoding of text as either dense or sparse vectors. Sparse vectors, which encode the identity of a word, are typically dictionary-length and contain mostly zeros. Dense vectors, which encode meaning, are more compact and contain fewer zeros. Various enhancements can improve the way similarities are calculated in the vector stores (databases).[9]
- Performance improves by optimizing how vector similarities are calculated. Dot products enhance similarity scoring, while approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) searches improve retrieval efficiency over K-nearest neighbors (KNN) searches.[10]
- Accuracy may be improved with Late Interactions, which allow the system to compare words more precisely after retrieval. This helps refine document ranking and improve search relevance.[11]
- Hybrid vector approaches may be used to combine dense vector representations with sparse one-hot vectors, taking advantage of the computational efficiency of sparse dot products over dense vector operations.[9]
- Other retrieval techniques focus on improving accuracy by refining how documents are selected. Some retrieval methods combine sparse representations, such as SPLADE, with query expansion strategies to improve search accuracy and recall.[12]

### Purpose and Key Information Comparison

#### Working-Time Declaration
- **Purpose**: To maintain records of the Working Time of mobile workers involved in operations subject to EU drivers' hours rules.
- **Key Points**:
  - **Reference Period**: Calculated over a 26-week calendar reference period.
    - Period 1: January 1 to June 30 (26 weeks)
    - Period 2: July 1 to December 31 (26 weeks)
  - **Maximum Average Working Time**: 48 hours per week over the 26-week reference period.
    - Can be extended to 26 weeks in certain circumstances.
  - **Weekly Limit**: Maximum of 60 hours Working Time.
  - **Night Work**: Maximum of 10 hours within each 24-hour period.
    - Defined as midnight to 0400 hours for goods vehicles and 0100 to 0500 hours for passenger vehicles.
  - **Rest Periods**: Mandatory breaks:
    - 30 minutes after 6 hours of Working Time.
    - 45 minutes after 9 hours of Working Time.
  - **Additional Declarations**: Both transport and non-transport working time must be declared.
  - **Charitable/Voluntary Work**: Must be reported and treated as regular work for the purpose of calculating Working Time.

#### RAG Article
- **Purpose**: To enhance large language models (LLMs) by incorporating an information-retrieval mechanism that allows models to access and utilize additional data beyond their original training set.
- **Key Points**:
  - **Enhancement**: Improves LLM performance by incorporating new information from external data sources.
  - **Process**:
    - Documents are converted into LLM embeddings.
    - Embeddings are stored in a vector database for retrieval.
    - Given a user query, a document retriever selects the most relevant documents to augment the query.
  - **Limitations**:
    - LLMs can still provide incorrect information, even when drawing from factually correct sources.
    - Context misinterpretation can lead to false statements.
  - **Improvements**:
    - Encoder methods focus on encoding text as either dense or sparse vectors.
    - Performance improvements through optimized vector similarity calculations.
    - Accuracy improvements through late interactions and hybrid vector approaches.
  - **Applications**: Used in applications requiring grounded responses in external or frequently updated information.

### Summary
Both the working-time declaration and the RAG article aim to manage and utilize data effectively. However, they serve different purposes and operate in distinct domains. The working-time declaration focuses on regulatory compliance and maintaining accurate records of working hours, while the RAG article aims to enhance the functionality of AI models by integrating external data sources.

These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]

Retriever-centric methods
[edit]These methods aim to enhance the quality of document retrieval in vector databases:
- Pre-training the retriever using the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), a technique that helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents.[13]
- Supervised retriever optimization aligns retrieval probabilities with the generator model's likelihood distribution. This involves retrieving the top-k vectors for a given prompt, scoring the generated response's perplexity, and minimizing KL divergence between the retriever's selections and the model's likelihoods to refine retrieval.[14]
- Reranking techniques can refine retriever performance by prioritizing the most relevant retrieved documents during training.[15]
Language model
[edit]By redesigning the language model with the retriever in mind, a 25-time smaller network can get comparable perplexity as its much larger counterparts.[16] Because it is trained from scratch, this method (Retro) incurs the high cost of training runs that the original RAG scheme avoided. The hypothesis is that by giving domain knowledge during training, Retro needs less focus on the domain and can devote its smaller weight resources only to language semantics. The redesigned language model is shown here.
It has been reported that Retro is not reproducible, so modifications were made to make it so. The more reproducible version is called Retro++ and includes in-context RAG.[17]

Chunking
[edit]Chunking involves various strategies for breaking up the data into vectors so the retriever can find details in it.
Hybrid search
[edit]Sometimes vector database searches (aka semantic search technique) can miss key facts needed to answer a user's question. One way to mitigate this is to do a traditional text search (aka full text search), combine those results to the text chunks linked to the retrieved vectors from the vector search, and feed the combined hybrid text (using effective scoring or reranking scoring) into the language model for generation.[18]
Challenges

[edit]Typically, the data to be referenced is converted into LLM embeddings, numerical representations in the form of a large vector space. RAG can be used on unstructured (usually text), semi-structured, or structured data (for example knowledge graphs). Improvements
[edit]Improvements to the basic process above can be applied at different stages in the RAG flow.
Encoder
[edit]These methods focus on the encoding of text as either dense or sparse vectors. Sparse vectors, which encode the identity of a word, are typically dictionary-length and contain mostly zeros. Dense vectors, which encode meaning, are more compact and contain fewer zeros. Various enhancements can improve the way similarities are calculated in the vector stores (databases).[9]
- Performance improves by optimizing how vector similarities are calculated. Dot products enhance similarity scoring, while approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) searches improve retrieval efficiency over K-nearest neighbors (KNN) searches.[10]
- Accuracy may be improved with Late Interactions, which allow the system to compare words more precisely after retrieval. This helps refine document ranking and improve search relevance.[11]
- Hybrid vector approaches may be used to combine dense vector representations with sparse one-hot vectors, taking advantage of the computational efficiency of sparse dot products over dense vector operations.[9]
- Other retrieval techniques focus on improving accuracy by refining how documents are selected. Some retrieval methods combine sparse representations, such as SPLADE, with query expansion strategies to improve search accuracy and recall.[12]

RAG poisoning
[edit]RAG systems may retrieve factually correct but misleading sources, leading to errors in interpretation. In some cases, an LLM may extract statements from a source without considering its context, resulting in an incorrect conclusion. Additionally, when faced with conflicting information, RAG models may struggle to determine which source is accurate. The worst case outcome of this limitation is that the model may combine details from multiple sources producing responses that merge outdated and updated information in a misleading manner. According to the MIT Technology Review, these issues occur because RAG systems may misinterpret the data they retrieve.[3]

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
RAG and LLM limitations
[edit]LLMs can provide incorrect information. For example, when Google first demonstrated its LLM tool "Bard" (later re-branded to Google Gemini), the LLM provided incorrect information about the James Webb Space Telescope. This error contributed to a $100 billion decline in Google's stock value.[5] RAG is used to prevent these errors, but it does not solve all the problems. For example, LLMs can generate misinformation even when pulling from factually correct sources if they misinterpret the context. MIT Technology Review gives the example of an AI-generated response stating, "The United States has had one Muslim president, Barack Hussein Obama." The model retrieved this from the rhetorical chapter title "Barack Hussein Obama: America's First Muslim President?" in the book Faith in the New Millennium: The Future of Religion and American Politics.[6] The LLM did not "know" or "understand" the context of the title, generating a false statement.[3]
LLMs with RAG are programmed to prioritize new information. This technique has been called "prompt stuffing." Without prompt stuffing, the LLM's input is generated by a user; with prompt stuffing, additional relevant context is added to this input to guide the model's response. This approach provides the LLM with key information early in the prompt, encouraging it to prioritize the supplied data over pre-existing training knowledge.[7]

The model feeds this relevant retrieved information into the LLM via prompt engineering of the user's original query. Newer implementations (as of 2023[update]) can also incorporate specific augmentation modules with abilities such as expanding queries into multiple domains and using memory and self-improvement to learn from previous retrievals.[citation needed]

Applications
[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation is used in applications where generated responses need to be grounded in external or frequently updated information.[citation needed]
In healthcare, RAG has been studied as a way to ground large language model outputs in external medical knowledge sources, although reviews have noted continuing challenges around evaluation, ethics, and clinical reliability.[8]

Retriever-centric methods
[edit]These methods aim to enhance the quality of document retrieval in vector databases:
- Pre-training the retriever using the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), a technique that helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents.[13]
- Supervised retriever optimization aligns retrieval probabilities with the generator model's likelihood distribution. This involves retrieving the top-k vectors for a given prompt, scoring the generated response's perplexity, and minimizing KL divergence between the retriever's selections and the model's likelihoods to refine retrieval.[14]
- Reranking techniques can refine retriever performance by prioritizing the most relevant retrieved documents during training.[15]
Language model
[edit]By redesigning the language model with the retriever in mind, a 25-time smaller network can get comparable perplexity as its much larger counterparts.[16] Because it is trained from scratch, this method (Retro) incurs the high cost of training runs that the original RAG scheme avoided. The hypothesis is that by giving domain knowledge during training, Retro needs less focus on the domain and can devote its smaller weight resources only to language semantics. It has been reported that Retro is not reproducible, so modifications were made to make it so. The more reproducible version is called Retro++ and includes in-context RAG.[17]

Improvements
[edit]Improvements to the basic process above can be applied at different stages in the RAG flow.
Encoder
[edit]These methods focus on the encoding of text as either dense or sparse vectors. Sparse vectors, which encode the identity of a word, are typically dictionary-length and contain mostly zeros. Dense vectors, which encode meaning, are more compact and contain fewer zeros. Various enhancements can improve the way similarities are calculated in the vector stores (databases).[9]
- Performance improves by optimizing how vector similarities are calculated. Dot products enhance similarity scoring, while approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) searches improve retrieval efficiency over K-nearest neighbors (KNN) searches.[10]
- Accuracy may be improved with Late Interactions, which allow the system to compare words more precisely after retrieval. This helps refine document ranking and improve search relevance.[11]
- Hybrid vector approaches may be used to combine dense vector representations with sparse one-hot vectors, taking advantage of the computational efficiency of sparse dot products over dense vector operations.[9]
- Other retrieval techniques focus on improving accuracy by refining how documents are selected. Some retrieval methods combine sparse representations, such as SPLADE, with query expansion strategies to improve search accuracy and recall.[12]

Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.[1][2] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]
